subject: Banking
title: The South Sea Bubble
description: A fast breakdown of The South Sea Bubble for builders.

hook.text: In 1720, the South Sea Company promised investors riches from trade. Its stock rose 800% before crashing to nothing.

buildup.text: The British government let the company take over national debt.

discovery.text: The company had almost no real trade revenue. The stock price was pure speculation fed by insider manipulation.

twist.text: Isaac Newton invested early, sold for a profit, then reinvested near the peak and lost £20,000 — a fortune at the time.

climax.text: Even a genius couldn't resist the bubble. The South Sea crash proved that herd behavior defeats individual intelligence.

punchline.text: Newton lost a fortune. The South Sea Bubble defeated even genius.

quiz.question: What happened to Isaac Newton during the South Sea Bubble?
options: He sold at a profit then reinvested near the peak and lost £20,000

details.summary: The South Sea Bubble of 1720 was a British speculative mania where shares in the South Sea Company rose tenfold based on impossible promises of trading wealth. The bubble's collapse ruined thousands, including Isaac Newton.
details.whyItMatters: The South Sea Bubble is one of history's most important financial manias, demonstrating that speculative bubbles are as old as financial markets. Isaac Newton's famous loss shows that intelligence does not protect against market psychology.
takeaways: South Sea Company shares rose from £128 to over £1,000 in six months
Isaac Newton lost £20,000, equivalent to millions in modern currency
The collapse led to the Bubble Act restricting new company formations

faq.question: What was the South Sea Company actually worth?
faq.answer: Almost nothing in real business terms. The company had a monopoly on trade with South America but barely traded there. Its true business was a scheme to refinance government debt. Share prices were driven entirely by speculation and insider manipulation.

faq.question: What did Isaac Newton learn from the bubble?
faq.answer: Newton initially sold his shares for a £7,000 profit, then bought back in near the peak and lost £20,000. He reportedly said he could calculate the motions of heavenly bodies but not the madness of people, a lasting lesson about market psychology.
